doc: The observability vocabulary, shared by every Halyard service in every language.
SPEC 17.3 asks for one trace and one log search that span five hops: console,
api, sandboxd, the sandbox, and the tool call. Two of those hops are Go and
two are Python. If the Go side writes org_id and the Python side writes orgId,
or if one tags spans halyard.org.id and the other halyard.org_id, that search
silently returns half the story — the worst possible failure for a debugging
tool, because it looks like an answer.
The redaction lists have a sharper version of the same problem. A denylist that
exists in Go and is retyped in Python is a denylist that will be updated in Go
and not in Python, and the leak will surface in whichever service was forgotten.
packages/chassis/logging/tripwire.go said so before this file existed: 'two
copies will diverge, and the copy that goes stale will be the one guarding the
more important boundary.'
So this is the single source. scripts/gen.sh compiles it into Go and Python
constants, docs and all, and make gen-check fails the build if the checked-in
output disagrees. Task 2.13's gitd pre-receive scanner reads secret_prefixes
from here rather than growing a third copy.
Editing rule: change this file, run make gen, commit both. Never edit a
generated file.

redacted.doc: Replaces a secret value. Searchable on purpose: counting these tells you how often callers try to log credentials.

suppressed_message.doc: Replaces a log message that contained a credential shape. The line is still emitted — dropping it entirely would hide the fact that something tried to log a secret, which is itself worth knowing.
suppressed_message.value: log line suppressed: it contained a credential-shaped literal

doc: The closed vocabulary of structured log field names.
It is closed so that a rename is one edit rather than a grep, and so that the
redaction audit test has something finite to iterate: every key here is
asserted not to be classified as a secret, which is what stops the denylist's
substring matching from silently swallowing a field a debugger needed.

groups.name: Correlation
groups.doc: SPEC 17.3 wants a trace spanning five hops; these are the fields that let a log search join onto it.

groups.name: HTTP
groups.doc: Route, never path: a raw path is unbounded cardinality and can carry a token or a user-chosen slug.

doc: Substrings that classify a log key as secret-bearing.
Substring matching is deliberately broad: a new provider's SDK will invent a
field name nobody predicted, and over-redacting a field is recoverable while
leaking a credential is not.
Keys rescued from the denylist. Checked first.
This list is load-bearing: without it "key" alone eats idempotency_key and
cache_key, and "auth" eats author. A test in each language ties it to the
log_keys vocabulary above, so a new field name that the denylist would
swallow fails the build rather than going quietly missing from your logs.
Literal credential shapes, scanned for in the message text itself.
This closes the one hole key matching cannot: a token interpolated into a
message by a library we do not own, as in
log.Printf("auth failed for token=%s", tok).
Literal prefixes only — no regular expressions. Measured at ~172ns with zero
allocations on a clean string in Go, which is cheap enough to run on every
line.
Task 2.13's gitd pre-receive secret scanner reads this same list.

groups.name: Connection strings, which carry a password inline

doc: Span attribute and baggage keys carrying the SPEC 17.3 tenancy tuple.
Dotted segments follow OTel convention: an entity's id gets its own segment,
as in service.instance.id, and snake_case is reserved for multi-word leaves.
So halyard.org.id, not halyard.org_id.
Identical strings to the span attributes, named separately so a future
divergence is expressible without a silent rename.
